title: Devilled Kidneys
subtitle: Lamb kidneys in a hot, mustardy butter sauce on toast
excerpt: Lamb kidneys quickly fried in butter with Worcestershire sauce, mustard, and cayenne until just cooked, then served on hot toast. A Victorian breakfast dish that is still one of the best uses for offal.

recipe.sourceNotes: Devilled kidneys were a staple of the Victorian and Edwardian breakfast table, served from the sideboard at country house breakfasts alongside kedgeree and smoked haddock. 'Devilling' refers to any preparation with a sharp, pungent seasoning — typically mustard, cayenne, and Worcestershire sauce — that gives a hot, aggressive flavour. The dish fell out of fashion in the mid-20th century along with the culture of elaborate breakfasts, but has been revived by British chefs interested in offal and nose-to-tail cooking. Lamb kidneys are mild enough to be approachable for those new to offal.

content.text: The kidneys must be cooked at high heat for a very short time: overcooking makes them rubbery and strong-tasting. They are done when the outside is browned and the inside is just barely pink. Cut them in half and remove the white core (the ureter) before cooking or they will be bitter. Have the toast ready before you start cooking the kidneys.
Mix together the Worcestershire sauce, mustard, cayenne, and lemon juice. Pat the kidney halves dry with kitchen paper. Season lightly with salt.
Heat the butter in a heavy pan over high heat until foaming. Add the kidneys cut-side down. Fry for 2 minutes without moving, until well browned. Turn and cook for 1 to 2 minutes on the other side.
Pour the devilling sauce over the kidneys. Toss for 30 seconds. Remove from the heat. Scatter with parsley. Spoon onto hot buttered toast and serve immediately.
